name: Thickening spray

lead: Thickening sprays are styling products that coat strands with polymers, proteins or light resins so hair looks wider and fuller, with more grip and root volume. They are aimed at fine or thinning hair.

Film-forming polymers deposit on the shaft, thickening it and adding friction between strands so hair stands off the scalp. Combined with heat styling, this creates root lift that makes hair look denser. The effect is cosmetic and washes out, and the products are not claimed to change growth.

paras: Applied to damp hair before blow-drying or to dry hair for texture, usually as part of a thin-hair styling routine. Many people pair it with a blow dryer for lift at the roots. The look lasts until the next wash.

Reported issues include product build-up, stiffness, dryness and occasional scalp reactions to fragrance or alcohol. There are few clinical studies of thickening sprays as a class, and claims are limited to appearance.

web.title: Hair Thickening Spray: How Does It Work? (Wimpole)

angle.text: People with fine or thinning hair spray thickening products for root volume and fuller-looking strands. Polymers or proteins coat each strand so it looks wider and holds lift. The effect is cosmetic and lasts until the next wash; the products are not claimed to change growth.

lead: Thickening sprays are styling products applied to damp or dry hair to make strands look wider and fuller and to add volume and grip at the roots. They are aimed at fine or thinning hair, where the goal is a denser-looking head of hair for a day, until the next wash. The effect is cosmetic: manufacturers present them as covering or coating existing hair rather than altering growth.[1][2]

Two broad types are described. Coating sprays deposit polymers, proteins or light resins on each strand so it looks thicker and has more friction and lift. Concealer or fibre sprays use fine particles or keratin fibres that cling to hair and scalp to hide gaps.[2][3] Spray-on hair, sold as "hair in a can", was popularised in the 1980s by Ronco's GLH-9 and later by infomercials.[3]

Thickening sprays belong to the wider film-forming family that includes hair spray, which Grokipedia describes as formulations of polymers, solvents and propellants leaving a thin adhesive layer on strands.[4] No clinical study of thickening sprays as a class was identified; a published patient-satisfaction study has examined topical hair fibre fillers, a related camouflage product.[5]
infobox: Coating polymers or proteins; some products use fibres or particles
Fine or thinning hair; also after hair transplants

paras: Thickening sprays are sold as pump or aerosol products and are applied to damp hair before blow-drying or to dry hair for texture. They are used by people with fine or thinning hair who want more apparent density, and some people also use them with other camouflage products such as hair fibres.[5] A hair-transplant clinic's explainer also lists people with thinning or receding hair, people using longer-term treatments, and people in the early stage after a transplant as typical users.[2]

Grokipedia's account of hair sprays says that polymers such as polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) and acrylate copolymers form a film that sets hold and resists humidity, delivered in an alcohol or water carrier, with aerosol versions using propellants such as dimethyl ether.[4] Wikipedia's article on hair spray similarly lists polymer concentrates, plasticizers, fragrances and propellants as the components.[1] In thickening products the same film-forming approach adds coating to each strand and friction between strands, which proponents say lifts hair away from the scalp, especially with blow-drying.

Fibre-type products are described by one clinic as using keratin fibres that bind to hair through static charge and come in shades from white and grey to black, matched to the user's hair.[2] Thickening shampoos and conditioners are described as swelling the hair shaft to add apparent volume until the next wash, and regular use can cause build-up that dulls hair.[2] Spray-on hair products colour the scalp and thicken existing hair, or form fibres that cling to the scalp and hair.[3]

Early hair sprays were developed in Europe in the 1920s, and aerosol hair sprays followed in the US around the 1940s, with Chase Products first packaging one in 1948.[1] Chlorofluorocarbon propellants were phased out in the 1980s and replaced by hydrocarbons.[1] Ronco's GLH-9 ("Great Looking Hair Formula #9"), a spray-on hair product, was pioneered in the 1980s and sold over half a million cans after 1990s infomercials.[3] Volumizing and thickening variants are later marketing categories within this lineage.

Grokipedia notes that hair-spray formulations raise respiratory irritation concerns on inhalation and flammability concerns around residues.[4] Product build-up, stiffness, dryness and scalp reactions to fragrance or alcohol are commonly listed as possible drawbacks of styling sprays; published clinical data for thickening sprays specifically are limited.
No studies found for thickening sprays. A published cross-sectional study of patient satisfaction and adverse effects with topical hair fibre fillers examined a related camouflage product.[5]

Archived r/tressless searches on hair fibres show that thickening and fixing products come up in discussion of camouflage routines.[6] Users there tend to describe these as cosmetic cover while using other treatments.

lore.intro: Thickening sprays and fibres appear in hair-loss communities as camouflage used while pursuing other treatments.[6]

claims.claim: Thickening sprays make thin hair look fuller for a day.
Sprays change hair growth over time.

timeline.event: Early hair sprays developed in Europe.[1]
Aerosol and resin-based hair sprays appear in the US.[1][4]
Spray-on hair products such as Ronco's GLH-9 are introduced; CFC propellants phased out.[1][3]
Spray-on hair sold widely through infomercials.[3]
